issues.legal_issue: The exemption for a qualifying residential palace applies to the annual value of the whole palace even when part of it is occupied by a tenant and the ruler occupies the remainder as a residence.
material_facts: The taxpayer owned a palace declared by the Central Government to be his official residence and inalienable ancestral property.
The taxpayer used part of the palace as his residence, while the Defence Ministry occupied a requisitioned portion and paid rent.
The dispute arose in income-tax assessment proceedings over whether the rental income from the occupied portion was taxable.
issues.conclusion: The annual value of the whole palace was exempt, including the portion occupied by the tenant; the palace could not be split to confine the exemption to the portion used by the ruler as a residence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 10(19A) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, read with paragraph 15(iii) of the Part B States (Taxation Concessions) Order, 1950, the exemption applies where the ruler owns the palace as ancestral property, occupies it as a residence, and the Central Government has declared it exempt. The word “palace” in Section 10(19A) does not permit splitting it into portions: unlike Section 5(iii) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, and Sections 23(2) and 23(3) of the Income Tax Act, it does not refer to a building or a house or part of a house. Once the statutory conditions for exemption are satisfied, the exemption provision is construed liberally. The Court approved CIT v. Bharatchandra Banjdeo and CIT v. H.H. Maharao Bhim Singhji, and rejected the contrary view in Maharawal Laxman Singh v. CIT.

rule.if: income_tax_exemption_proceeding and qualifying_ancestral_palace and palace_declared_exempt and ruler_uses_palace_as_residence and part_occupied_by_tenant

predicates.income_tax_exemption_proceeding: The dispute arises in an income-tax assessment proceeding about whether income from a palace is exempt.
predicates.qualifying_ancestral_palace: A ruler owns the palace as ancestral property.
predicates.palace_declared_exempt: The Central Government has declared the palace exempt as the ruler’s official residence.
predicates.ruler_uses_palace_as_residence: The ruler occupies and uses some of the palace as a residence.
predicates.part_occupied_by_tenant: A tenant occupies part of the palace and pays rent for it.
predicates.whole_palace_annual_value_exempt: The annual value of the whole palace, including the tenant-occupied portion, is exempt.

issues.definition: When an income-tax exemption dispute concerns a declared ancestral palace used as a residence by its ruler, the exemption covers the whole palace even if a tenant occupies part of it.

issues.legal_issue: A revenue authority should not pursue the same income-tax issue in higher courts after it has been decided on the merits by a higher court in earlier assessment proceedings, absent a valid and convincing reason.
material_facts: The same exemption issue had been decided in the taxpayer’s favour for earlier assessment years.
The earlier decision of the High Court had been affirmed when the Revenue’s special leave petition was dismissed.
The Revenue pursued the same issue again for a later assessment year, and the Court found no valid or convincing reason for doing so.
issues.conclusion: Although res judicata does not apply to income-tax proceedings and each assessment year is independent, there was no justification for the Revenue to pursue the issue again in the higher courts after it had been decided on the merits.
issues.legal_principle: Each assessment year is independent and res judicata does not apply to income-tax proceedings, but finality should attach to an issue once it has been decided on the merits by higher courts. In the absence of a valid and convincing reason, the Revenue should not pursue the same issue again. The Court relied on M/s Radhasoami Satsang, Saomi Bagh, Agra v. Commissioner of Income Tax.

predicates.income_tax_assessment_proceeding: The matter arises in income-tax assessment proceedings for a particular assessment year.
predicates.same_issue_decided_on_merits_by_higher_c: A higher court has already decided the same issue on its merits in earlier assessment proceedings.
predicates.no_valid_convincing_reason_for_renewal: No valid and convincing reason is given for pursuing the same issue again.
predicates.revenue_should_not_pursue_same_issue_aga: The Revenue should not pursue the same issue again in the higher courts.

issues.definition: If a higher court has decided the same income-tax issue on its merits and there is no valid and convincing reason to renew it, the Revenue should not pursue it again.

issues.legal_issue: The validity of property requisition proceedings cannot be determined in an appeal arising from income-tax proceedings when that issue is unrelated to the tax dispute.
material_facts: In the income-tax appeal, the taxpayer also challenged the continued occupation of the requisitioned property after the asserted expiry of the requisition period.
The appeal concerned the taxability of rental income, not the validity of the requisition or the continued possession of the property.
issues.conclusion: The requisition-related challenge was misplaced in the income-tax appeal and had to be raised in appropriate proceedings before a competent forum.
issues.legal_principle: A challenge to requisition proceedings must be brought before a competent forum in appropriate proceedings; it cannot be adjudicated in an appeal arising from an unrelated income-tax dispute.

predicates.income_tax_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from an income-tax dispute.
predicates.challenge_concerns_property_requisition: A party challenges the validity or continued effect of proceedings requisitioning property.
predicates.requisition_issue_unrelated_to_tax_dispu: The requisition challenge is unrelated to the tax issue before the court.
predicates.requisition_challenge_not_adjudicated_in: The requisition challenge is not adjudicated in the income-tax appeal and must be raised in appropriate proceedings before a competent forum.

issues.definition: When a property-requisition challenge is unrelated to the income-tax dispute in an appeal, the court does not adjudicate that challenge in the tax appeal.
